newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries under pressure amid supply spate.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries under pressure amid supply spate.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries will struggle to remain afloat over the next few weeks as a flood of fresh supply puts some downward pressure on prices, analysts said.
"The supply will weigh on the market to some extent," said Kevin Flanagan, economist and first vice-president at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

"It's tough to say for sure the burden of supply is going to curtail demand and you're going to have some very disturbing auction results. But it does place limits on how enthusiatic investors' reception will be," he added.

U.S. Treasury market players will have a lot to bid for over the next few weeks. Starting on January 22, the Treasury will offer the market $17.5 billion in two-year securities, followed by $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Thursday. On January 27, the Treasury will dump on the market some $23.0 billion during its weekly three- and six-month bill sale.

Shortly after, on January 29, the government will launch its first auction of the so-called "inflation notes." The Treasury will offer investors $7.0 billion in 10-year notes whose yields will be indexed to inflation so rising prices do not eat into their value upon maturity.
Auctions of these new instruments will be held on a quarterly basis.
Following the supply calendar, the Treasury is expected to announce the details of its quarterly refunding on February 5.
The refunding effort, which will include the sale of three- and 10-year notes and 30-year bonds, is expected to take place on February 11, 12 and 13.
On top of that, issuance of corporate bonds has also been on the strong side, amounting more than $10 billion over the last two weeks, analysts said.

Although the amount of money involved in the auctions -- $60 billion excluding the to-be-announced refunding effort -- appears to be intimidating, some analysts said the fundamental conditions of the U.S. economy might encourage the purchase of Treasuries.

Experts said a recent strength of the U.S. dollar against other major currencies combined with some positive signs on the budget deficit reduction front might help the assimilation of the new securities.
"The strength of dollar ... implies that there is and there will be an active foreign demand for the new issues," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
"Friendly-sounding comments on (U.S.) deficit reduction is also positive at this time," Moran added.

Moran was referring to recent comments by president Clinton suggesting that he would be willing to larger cuts in Medicare that he was before. Some Republicans leaders in the Senate received Clinton's proposal warmly.
"I think this would be a positive for the market and help the auctions go well ... We are not likely to see much of a backup in interest rates," Moran said.

From all the securities to be sold, the new "inflation notes" are seen as the most peculiar one. "This is a new instrument and we still don't know how it's going to perform. I think nobody does," said a trader at a major U.S. primary dealership.
Pundits said the profile of the potential buyer of the new inflation-indexed instrument is likely to be different from the yield-starved, day-trade speculator on Wall Street.
They said retailers, some corporations and long-term pension funds, such as 401K retirement plans, would be the likely bidders at the 10-year inflation-indexed notes.

"There will be some individuals, there will some corporations that will need to match liabilities ... But it looks to me that the size of the auction is a bit larger that would've been ideal," said Lee Youngdahl, vice-president at Aubrey G. Lanston.
Institutional players are not seen as active bidders. "I don't think institutions really want it...Demand will have to come from the retail sector," Dean Witter's Flanagan said.
